Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
324 AM EDT Wed Aug 12 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 309 AM EDT Wednesday...

No Significant changes were made. Isolated to scattered showers
with a few embedded thunderstorms are expected today. 

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 309 AM EDT Wednesday...

1. Isolated to scattered showers are expected this afternoon
with a few thunderstorms mixed in. Chances increase Thursday
as a wave moves through with lingering showers Friday. 

2. Tranquil weather on Saturday, then beneficial rain likely 
spreads in from the west Sunday afternoon and exits on Monday. 
Becoming seasonably warm and dry early next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 309 AM EDT Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Maintained yesterday's forecast change of
including some showers and very isolated convection today. Best
chances of thunderstorms lie in the St Lawrence Valley where the
CAPE gradient will be sharpest with around 500J/kg to work with.
Otherwise, temperatures will be similar to yesterday with highs
in the mid/upper 70s to low 80s today and Thursday. Shower and 
thunderstorm chances increase Thursday as low pressure moving 
through southern Canada pushes a boundary through the region.
Around 500 J/kg of CAPE is projected to be in the region
coincident with the weakening boundary with the strongest
forcing towards the Canadian border(CAMs are highlighting 
potential for a bullseye of 1000+J/kg at max heating which may 
strafe our northern zones in Vermont - lower likelihood, but 
potentially impactful scenario where a couple stronger storms 
would be possible). Another trough is anticipated to move 
through Friday in broad northwest flow. Showers are mostly 
expected, but could see a few rumbles in southern Vermont where 
timing will play a roll in convective chances. Should the trough
slow, surface instability will likely build enough for more 
showers and storms, but current timing of this wave supports 
mainly showers as the wave exists early afternoon. Some breezy
conditions should be anticipated with this trough, especially on
Lake Champlain and the peaks where gusts could approach or 
exceed 30 mph. Gusts 15 to 25 mph are probable at lower
elevations away from Lake Champlain. 

KEY MESSAGE 2: A mid-level ridge over the southeastern US will 
build northward a bit on Saturday, leaving us in northwesterly 
flow with dry air and no precipitation chances. This ridge will 
breakdown on Sunday, allowing a weak wave of low pressure 
originating in the foothills of the Colorado Rockies to zip 
eastward and bring us some overrunning/warm frontal type of 
rain. There is a slight chance of thunder indicated at this time
Sunday night in much of Vermont, which would only be a factor 
if the low pressure system trended stronger and/or tracked 
farther north, such that our region got into the system's warm 
sector. Otherwise, a steady soaking rain looks favored, with 
current consensus timing from Sunday afternoon through Monday 
morning. Probabilities of event total rainfall exceeding 0.5" 
currently ranges from about 20% to 40%, tapering off generally 
towards the north. among the latest global ensemble scenarios, 
some solutions are a little slower to bring rain to an end on 
Monday with higher probabilities of rain into Monday evening 
than what the current forecast suggests. Given the 
uncertainties, the 10-30% chance of showers Monday afternoon 
looks reasonable at this time; some of this precipitation could 
be orographic, post-frontal showers. 

Following this system it appears a ridge of high pressure may build 
in, which would provide us with generally quiet weather for Tuesday. 
There are weak signals for perhaps a terrain-driven shower in the 
Adirondacks or off of a lake breeze interface, which would make 
sense given a typical summertime heating scenario with lack of other 
forcing mechanisms for precipitation.

&&

.AVIATION /07Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
Through 06Z Thursday...Dense fog will certainly be the main aviation
impact over the next six hours, particularly at fog-prone sites. At
SLK, intervals of fog have already begun. Would expect the typically
frequent LIFR conditions through about 12Z, with crossover
temperatures already met prior to 06Z. Mid-level clouds currently
are moving through northern Vermont which could delay fog formation
at EFK and MPV, but don't think it will linger all night based on
satellite trends. Otherwise, isolated to scattered showers with a
few thunderstorms are anticipated for much of the 18Z through 06Z
timeframe, with perhaps a greater likelihood of a direct hit at our
northern terminals (especially MSS, and perhaps PBG and BTV) based
on the latest guidance. Chances are too low to indicate in the TAFs
at this time. Winds aside from a thunderstorm or stronger shower
will be light; during the daytime, generally expect west/northwest
winds, except terrain driven in the Champlain Valley (SE at PBG,
N-NW at BTV).

Outlook...
